about: The Structural Design Project is a Part IA coursework project, running across Michaelmas, Lent and Easter terms, in which students work in pairs to design, manufacture and test a metal structure that carries given loads at minimum cost. Structures are tested to destruction in ascending order of cost, and students then recommend improvements. It is assessed on the tested product, the drawings and individual reports, and carries 42 coursework marks (qualifying level 28) under the 2026-27 credit notice.
topics: Drawings, the test and the report

notes.h: What the Structural Design Project is
notes.body:
The Structural Design Project is a Part IA coursework project that every student takes part in, running across Michaelmas, Lent and Easter terms. It is the first time you design something real against a specification and then see it tested.

The task (from the Part IA guide)
- Working in pairs, you design, manufacture and test a metal structure that must carry given loads at minimum cost.
- The structures are tested to destruction, in ascending order of their "cost".
- After the test, you make recommendations on how your design could have been improved.
- Assessment is based on the quality of the tested product, the quality of your drawings, and your individual reports.

What it has looked like in the past (2019 example, possibly out of date)
- A June 2019 news item from the department's Structures group reported 348 first-year students working in pairs on bridges and cantilevers, both straight and skewed, tested to destruction and judged on design, cost and strength. This is only an illustration from one past year: the brief can change, so rely on the handout for your year.

How it fits with the rest of Part IA
- It draws directly on 1P2 Structures (trusses, deflections, beams and buckling), on the drawing courses (computer-aided design and engineering drawing) and on report and presentation skills from Exposition.
- Because it runs across all three terms, much of the structural theory you need arrives while the project is under way; it is worth reading ahead in the 1P2 notes on trusses and column buckling.

Structural Design Project credit (2026-27 credit notice)
- Drawings: 12 marks.
- Construction and Test: 12 marks.
- Presentation and Report: 18 marks.
- Total 42 marks, with a qualifying level of 28. This is the largest single coursework item in Part IA.
- The Part IA guide describes assessment by the quality of the tested product, the quality of the drawings and the individual reports. Although you work in a pair, the reports are individual, so each of you must be able to explain and justify the design.

How Part IA coursework counts (2026-27 credit notice)
- All Part IA coursework is for standard credit. Once you reach the satisfactory standard, your marks for an activity are capped at its qualifying level, so there is no reward for going beyond it.
- The qualifying marks for all Part IA coursework add up to 200. The coursework mark that counts is your raw total minus 100, so it is at most 100.
- That is added to the four written papers, each marked out of 200, giving 900 marks in all for Part IA.
- You must complete every activity satisfactorily to get the full qualifying mark. Missing, late or unsatisfactory work leaves a shortfall, and the Part IA guide says shortfalls are deducted from your Tripos total.
- If illness or grave cause stops you completing coursework, the notice says you can apply to the EAMC for an allowance; for missed sessions, follow the department's rules on rearranging coursework and extensions.
- Submitted work must be your own, and any use of AI tools must follow University and departmental guidance.

The project is judged on carrying the load at minimum cost, so the aim is a structure that is just strong enough, with no wasted material. The following standard principles from 1P2 Structures are the ones most likely to matter; the specific loads, materials, cost rules and test rig come from your project handout.

Find the load path first
- Sketch how each load gets to the supports. A triangulated (pin-jointed) layout carries load mainly by axial force, which uses material far more efficiently than bending.
- A pin-jointed triangle cannot change shape without a bar changing length; a rectangle of pinned bars is a mechanism. Check the count b + r = 2j and look for mechanisms.

Analyse member forces
- Use the method of joints or sections to find which members are in tension and which in compression, and how large the forces are. Use symmetry to halve the work.
- Ties (tension): strength depends on area, so A = T/σ_allow, and ties can be slender.
- Struts (compression): usually limited by buckling, P_cr = π²EI/L_e². Because P_cr falls with the square of the effective length, halving a strut's length (for example by bracing it at midpoint) quadruples its buckling load.
- For the same area, a tube or angle puts material further from the axis than a solid bar, giving a larger I and a larger buckling load.
- Real members are imperfect, so do not design struts right up to the Euler load.

Check deflection
- Use virtual work (δ = Σ t e) to estimate how much the structure will deflect, especially if the brief limits deflection.

Do not forget the details
- Joints, connections and load points often fail before the members do. Think about how forces get into and out of each joint, and about eccentricity, which adds bending.
- Consider which member you expect to fail first, and at what load. Comparing that prediction with the test result is the core of a strong report.

Balance cost against safety margin
- Every margin costs money. Make deliberate, justified choices and record them: an honest comparison of predicted and actual behaviour is worth more in the report than a structure that happened to survive.

notes.h: Drawings, the test and the report
notes.body:
The marks are split across drawings, construction and test, and presentation and report, so plan your effort accordingly rather than concentrating only on the build.

Drawings
- Your drawings must be good enough for someone else to make the structure: dimensions, materials, joint details and member sizes, following the conventions taught in the CAD and engineering drawing courses.
- Check that the drawings match what you actually built, and update them if the design changes.

Construction and test
- Build carefully and accurately: misaligned members and poor joints introduce eccentric loads and imperfections that reduce strength, particularly of compression members.
- Before the test, write down your prediction: the failure load, the member or joint you expect to fail and the expected mode (yield, buckling, joint failure).
- Watch the test closely, and take photographs or notes of how the failure starts.

Presentation and report
- Explain the design concept and the alternatives you considered, show the structural calculations, compare predicted and observed behaviour, and explain any differences.
- Make specific, justified recommendations for improvement, as the Part IA guide requires; for example, which member to resize, re-brace or reconnect, and what effect that would have on cost and strength.
- The reports are individual. Each partner should understand the whole design, not just their half.
- Apply the Exposition habits: clear structure, a short summary, labelled figures with units, and honest discussion.

cards.f: Effect on Euler buckling load of halving a strut's effective length
cards.b: It multiplies the buckling load by 4, since P_cr = π²EI/L_e².
A pin-jointed triangle cannot change shape without a bar changing length, so loads are carried by axial forces; a rectangle of pinned bars is a mechanism.

cards.f: Tube versus solid bar of equal area as a strut
cards.b: The tube has material further from the axis, so a larger I and radius of gyration, and a higher buckling load for the same mass (provided the wall is not so thin that it buckles locally).

questions.q: A slender pin-ended strut in your design is predicted to buckle elastically. Which change multiplies its buckling load by about four?
options: Bracing it at mid-length so that its effective length halves
Changing to a material with twice the Young's modulus
Changing to a material with twice the yield stress
questions.why: P_cr = π²EI/L_e², so halving L_e multiplies P_cr by 4. Doubling the length divides it by 4. Doubling E only doubles P_cr. Yield stress does not appear in the elastic buckling load at all, although it matters for stocky members.
